content: The Copper Family is a group of singers specializing in traditional, unaccompanied English folk songs. They originally hail from Rottingdean, a village near Brighton in Sussex, England, though the core members of the family now reside in the nearby village of Peacehaven. The Copper Family has maintained a longstanding tradition of singing unaccompanied folk songs that have been passed down through multiple generations. Their unique style and repertoire first gained significant attention in 1898 when Kate Lee, a founding member of the Folk Song Society (which later became the English Folk Dance and Song Society), discovered them. Kate Lee, who was also a singer, recognized the exceptional nature of their music, as both the collection of folk songs and the practice of unaccompanied singing were relatively uncommon at the time. James Brasser Copper (1845–1924) and his brother Thomas (circa 1847–circa 1936) were made honorary members of the Folk Song Society. Brasser was encouraged to document the songs he knew, which helped preserve their repertoire. Brasser had two sons, John (circa 1879–1952) and Jim (1882–1954). In 1936, Jim Copper compiled an additional volume of songs. Jim had two children, Joyce (born 1910) and Bob (1915–2004). In 1950, Jim and Bob were invited to perform on the BBC Radio program Country Magazine. Over the following years, the BBC recorded more of their performances, including a feature titled The Life of James Copper, which aired in September 1951. John's son, Walter Ronald (known as Ron, circa 1913–1979), also became involved in the family tradition. Together, Jim, John, Ron, and Bob performed at prestigious venues such as the Royal Albert Hall. Their music reached a wider audience through the six-part television series Song Hunter, presented by Alan Lomax, which featured Jim, Bob, and Ron. Bob Copper authored several books about the family and their songs, starting with the highly regarded A Song For Every Season in 1971. This book was accompanied by a four-LP set, which has since become a collector's item. The recordings featured Bob and Ron singing alongside Bob’s daughter Jill and son John, thereby introducing another generation to the family tradition. After Ron's death, Jill’s husband Jon joined the group, and some of Bob's grandchildren began performing with the family. The six grandchildren—Jill’s children Mark, Andy, and Sean Barratt, as well as John’s children Ben, Lucy, and Tom Copper—now perform independently as The Young Coppers, continuing the family’s repertoire. Since the 1950s, numerous recordings of the Copper Family’s singing have been made, many of which remain available. One notable release is Come Write Me Down, which includes two booklets filled with biographical details. Bob Copper passed away in 2004, shortly after being awarded an MBE. The current generations of the Copper Family continue to perform unaccompanied traditional songs. In 2006, BBC Four aired an hour-long documentary about the family. They are also involved in The Imagined Village project, which explores the evolution of English folk music. Discography: Traditional Songs From Rottingdean (English Folk Dance & Song Society LP, 1963) A Song For Every Season (Leader 4LP box set, 1971) A Song For Every Season (Leader LP, selections from the box set, 1971) The Banks of Claudy (Folktrax LP, 1975) Twankydillo (Folktrax cassette, 1975) Sweet Rose In June (Topic LP, 1977) Come All You Bold Britons (Folktrax cassette, 1983) Adam and Eve (Folktrax cassette, 1983) Coppersongs: A Living Tradition (English Folk Dance & Song Society LP, 1987) Coppersongs 2 (CD, 1995) Coppersongs 3: The Legacy Continues (CD, circa 1998) Come Write Me Down (Topic CD, 2001) Further Reading: Bob Copper for the Sheer Joy of Singing (2008). In Talking to Kinky and Karlheinz 170 musicians get vocal on The Music Show, edited by Anni Heino, pages 171–185. Sydney: ABC Books. ISBN 9780733320088.
